The first speaker traced the exchange of letters between two mathematicians, noting how often the argument turned on questions of notation rather than substance. Symbols that look obvious to a modern reader were contested for decades, and the surviving notes show the same quantity written in four or five different ways. One member of the audience objected that this was a story about printing as much as about mathematics, since a printer who lacked a piece of type could force a change in a formula; the speaker agreed and added that several familiar signs entered the literature through exactly that route. A second talk considered the reception of the subject in the universities, where the new methods were taught alongside the older geometrical proofs. Students complained that the lectures moved too quickly, that the examples were chosen badly, and that the examinations asked for manipulations no one had explained. By the middle of the century the situation had changed, and the older proofs were kept mainly as exercises. The third speaker, who had spent years in the archives, argued that the textbooks did more to fix the notation than the original papers did, because students copied the textbooks and teachers copied the students. The audience enjoyed this part of the talk more than the rest, and the questions went on until the building had to be closed. Not everyone in the room was convinced.
